mean: to be vain about something and flaunt it
lit: to hang something on one's nose, where the nose, as in many idioms, stands for pride

near.diff: 鼻が高い is feeling proud, often with good reason (of a child, of one's work); 鼻にかける is flaunting an advantage in a way others dislike.

mean: (of affectation) to become tiresome and off-putting

mean: to outdo someone who looked down on one

mean: to show one's talent and rise above others
lit: to show the top of one's head above the crowd

story.text: The phrase goes back to the epitaph the Tang writer Han Yu composed for his friend Liu Zongyuan. Han Yu wrote that Liu, though still young, passed the imperial examination and 'stood out sharply, showing the top of his head', so that people said the Liu family had produced a fine son.

near.diff: 肩を並べる is reaching the level of those at the top; 頭角を現す is the moment of standing out from one's peers on the way up.

mean: flatly, without hearing the other side out

mean: to relax and stop trying so hard
lit: to let the tension go out of one's shoulders

use.how: Often as advice: 肩の力を抜いて (relax, don't try so hard). Said of someone stiff with nerves or over-effort; 肩の力が抜ける is the intransitive.

near.diff: 気を抜く is letting your attention slip, usually a fault; 肩の力を抜く is a good thing: dropping needless tension while still doing the work.

cue: Before her first big presentation, your colleague has rewritten her slides five times and is pale with nerves. You give her some advice.

ctx.s: 「緊張[きんちょう]しないで、{肩[かた]の力[ちから]を抜[ぬ]いて}。」
ctx.en: "Don't be nervous. Just relax."

ctx.s: 「完璧[かんぺき]じゃなくていいんだよ。もっと{肩[かた]の力[ちから]を抜[ぬ]こう}よ。」
ctx.en: "It doesn't have to be perfect. Ease up a bit."

ctx.s: 本番[ほんばん]で{肩[かた]の力[ちから]を抜[ぬ]いたら}、かえっていい演奏[えんそう]ができた。
ctx.en: When I relaxed for the actual performance, I ended up playing better.

ctx.s: 子育[こそだ]ては、{肩[かた]の力[ちから]を抜[ぬ]いて}楽[たの]しむくらいがちょうどいい。
ctx.en: With bringing up children, it's best to relax and enjoy it.

ctx.s: 一人暮[ひとりぐ]らしを始[はじ]めた頃[ころ]は頑張[がんば]りすぎていたが、最近[さいきん]は{肩[かた]の力[ちから]を抜[ぬ]ける}ようになった。
ctx.en: When I first started living alone I tried far too hard, but lately I've learned to take it easy.

ctx.s: 先輩[せんぱい]の「失敗[しっぱい]してもいいよ」という一言[ひとこと]で{肩[かた]の力[ちから]が抜[ぬ]けて}、落[お]ち着[つ]いて話[はな]せた。
ctx.en: My senior's words, "It's fine if you fail," took the tension out of me, and I could speak calmly.

bad.s: 試合[しあい]に負[ま]けて、彼[かれ]はがっくりと{肩[かた]の力[ちから]を抜[ぬ]いた}。
bad.en: (meant: he lost the match and his shoulders slumped in disappointment)
bad.why: Slumping in disappointment is kata wo otosu. Kata no chikara wo nuku is letting go of needless tension, not a show of dejection.

bad.s: 面倒[めんどう]だったので、宿題[しゅくだい]は{肩[かた]の力[ちから]を抜[ぬ]いて}適当[てきとう]に済[す]ませた。
bad.en: (meant: it was a chore, so I cut corners and did my homework any old way)
bad.why: Doing sloppy work on purpose is te wo nuku. Kata no chikara wo nuku means dropping needless tension, not doing less.
